summary: The note reports on how increasingly severe, climate-driven weather is causing transit delays and cancellations in major cities, with case studies from New York, San Francisco, Chicago, Atlanta and Seattle. It covers economic costs, safety and accessibility concerns for vulnerable riders, and the human toll on commuters. It concludes that resilient infrastructure, technology, green transit and collective action are needed to adapt.
one_line: Weather-related transit disruptions in several US cities strain economies and commuters, prompting calls for resilient infrastructure, green transit and collective policy action.
key_facts: An unprecedented East Coast blizzard on September 14 was described by meteorologists as a once-in-a-decade event.
The West Coast has faced wildfires and heatwaves that caused rolling blackouts affecting electrically powered transit systems.
In New York City the blizzard struck on a Monday morning, halting subways, stranding thousands of commuters and leaving buses unable to navigate snow-clogged streets.
Jennifer S. Abbott, MTA Chief Operating Officer, said "the city's transportation infrastructure was pushed beyond its limits."
On October 3 in San Francisco, a major power outage aggravated by extreme heatwaves shut down BART for several hours, disrupting tech workers' commutes to Silicon Valley.
Economist Dr. Harold Peng said halted public transportation ripples through the economy, reducing business productivity and hitting hourly wage workers directly.
Weather emergencies incur substantial repair and upgrade costs for transit systems, with funds often diverted from other critical infrastructure projects.
During the November 5 snowstorm in Chicago, passengers were reportedly trapped on a train for several hours with little to no heat; Maria Gonzalez called for better emergency response plans.
Individuals with disabilities and older adults are disproportionately affected by service disruptions.
On December 10, Jane Richardson, director of Emergency Management for Atlanta's MARTA, admitted existing infrastructure was not designed for the severity and frequency of current weather events.
Samuel Lee's daughter missed a college entrance examination because of a flood-related train delay on January 15.
Seattle's transit authority is deploying electric buses with batteries able to withstand extreme temperature variations.
Thomas Klein of the "Transit for Future" campaign urges an immediate increase in funding and political will for a weather-resilient public transit network.
